title: Protection Is Not One Event:A Survey of RAG Protection Researchby Measured Endpoint

paper.title: Protection Is Not One Event: A Survey of RAG Protection Research by Measured Endpoint
paper.abstract: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems face security, privacy, and copyright risks including content leakage, source reconstruction, unauthorized access, data poisoning, and prompt injection. Yet RAG protection studies use incompatible evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models. We present a systematic survey and human-coded evidence map of 118 full-text-confirmed RAG defense papers, organized by measured endpoint rather than claimed goal or defense mechanism. Our seven-family taxonomy covers content disclosure, formal privacy proxies, access control and suppression, corpus-use detection, and pipeline integrity and attribution. Thirty-two annotators double-coded the papers ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ). The survey identifies three gaps. First, retrieval reranking and context rewriting each span five or six endpoint families, so mechanisms do not identify protection outcomes. Second, only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary endpoint; under the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% of records have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, and none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, most evaluations use general-purpose question-answering datasets and non-adaptive attacks rather than sensitive data and adaptive, multi-turn extraction. Our controlled RAG testbed shows that preventing verbatim copying does not prevent private-fact recovery: a normalized 8-gram guard reduces 20-token copying to 0.0%, but a three-query adaptive attacker recovers 48.3% of hidden facts on Qwen3-8B. We release the taxonomy, dataset, coding protocols, and testbed to enable comparable, claim-aligned RAG security evaluation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects language models to external document collections at inference time ( Lewis et al., 2020 ; Gao, 2023 ) . Because this external datastore can be searched, updated, and quoted directly, it creates new risks around privacy, copyright, and system security. Even if a document never appeared in pre-training, a RAG system might still leak its private details, copy its wording verbatim, or fall victim to poisoned entries. A rapidly growing literature aims to “protect” RAG systems against these risks, yet papers using this label rarely measure the same thing. Consider two studies that both claim to protect the copyright of a retrieval database. The first plants a watermark to prove after the fact that the database was queried, while the second blocks unauthorized users from retrieving restricted documents. A third study defends against poisoned passages to keep answers accurate, and a fourth rewrites retrieved text so the generator cannot copy it word for word. All four papers report successful “protection,” but they evaluate completely different technical events. Treating them as interchangeable, or pooling their scores to compare defenses, is like comparing a burglar alarm to a fireproof safe. Existing surveys organize this literature by threat model, pipeline stage, or system architecture. However, knowing where a defense sits in the pipeline tells us very little about what it actually achieves. In this work, we take a different approach: we survey RAG protection research based on the exact empirical endpoint each study measures. We define a frozen seven-family taxonomy of measured endpoints (Table A and Figure 1 ) that separates actual content disclosure from access control, usage detection, and pipeline integrity. Using this taxonomy, 32 annotators double-coded 118 full-text-confirmed RAG protection papers, reaching high agreement on what each paper measures ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ). Looking at the literature through its measured endpoints reveals three major blind spots. First, defense mechanisms only weakly predict what a paper tests (§ 5.1 ). Popular techniques such as retrieval reranking and context rewriting are evaluated across five or six different endpoint families, meaning readers cannot infer what was protected just from how the system was built. Second, research attention is heavily skewed away from actual data leakage (§ 5 ). Only 21 of the 118 papers (17.8%) have a primary endpoint that measures whether protected content is emitted to the user or reconstructed from the system. Among studies with the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, whereas none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, evaluation setups often fail to stress-test the defenses they propose (§ 5.3 ). Most studies rely on standard question-answering datasets that contain little sensitive content to begin with, and very few test against adaptive attackers who can ask follow-up questions. Our own controlled experiments confirm why this distinction matters: defenses that drive word-for-word copying down to zero still allow attackers to recover the underlying private facts (Appendix C ). To help future work build on clear empirical foundations, we make four contributions: • An endpoint-based survey that organizes RAG defense mechanisms, evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models by the exact technical event they measure (§ 4 , § 5.3 ). • A validated seven-family event taxonomy that makes cross-paper comparisons reproducible (§ 3 ). • A human-coded evidence map of 118 direct RAG protection papers, complete with item-level annotations, operating points, and open-source verification tools (§ 3 , Appendix D.2 ). • A critical audit and controlled testbed examining reporting quality, and the gap between stopping surface copying and preventing fact recovery (§ 5 , § 6 , Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Prior surveys of RAG security and privacy organize the field around system architecture and attack surfaces. Broad reviews of language model privacy cover threats like membership inference and data poisoning ( Das et al., 2025 ) alongside cryptographic and differentially private defenses ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . Dedicated surveys on copyright and ownership focus on text and model watermarking ( Yang et al., 2025 ) or fingerprinting techniques ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Within the RAG literature specifically, existing reviews group studies by threat model, pipeline stage, or defensive module ( Mu et al., 2026 ; Palanisamy et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . While this architectural view shows where a defense intervenes, it obscures what the evaluation actually tests. Individual empirical studies already hint at this divergence: papers evaluating literal and non-literal text reproduction ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , copyright-sensitive activation steering ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , proprietary knowledge base defense ( Li et al., 2026a ) , and knowledge extraction benchmarks ( Qi et al., 2026 ) all define “protection” through different operational outcomes. Furthermore, recent adaptation methods train models to decide when to retrieve, critique context, or withhold answers ( Asai et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) , blurring the boundary between parametric memory and external datastores. Rather than grouping papers by where their mechanisms sit in the pipeline, we human-code the exact technical events their experiments measure. Our approach builds on meta-scientific audits of machine learning research ( Lipton and Steinhardt, 2019 ; Kapoor and Narayanan, 2023 ) and classical measurement theory, which requires clearly defining target concepts and validating how they are measured ( Cronbach and Meehl, 1955 ; Campbell and Fiske, 1959 ; Messick, 1995 ) . These principles have shaped recent critiques of benchmark design and fairness evaluation in natural language processing ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ; Blodgett et al., 2021 ; Raji et al., 2021 ; Bowman and Dahl, 2021 ) . However, while prior audits typically expose flaws inside an experimental setup, we examine the link between two separate components of a paper: its high-level protection claim and its measured empirical endpoint. This focus on claim-measurement alignment parallels recent findings in question answering, where standard lexical overlap metrics often fail to capture true semantic accuracy ( Bulian et al., 2022 ; Kamalloo et al., 2023 ; Adlakha et al., 2024 ) . sections.heading: 3 The Endpoint Taxonomy and Human-Coded Evidence Map
sections.text: To compare RAG protection studies fairly, we first need a clear way to categorize what their experiments actually measure. Treating “protection” as a single outcome confuses very different technical events. Stopping a model from copying source text word for word is not the same as hiding personal identifiers, preventing attackers from inverting vector embeddings, proving a differential privacy bound, blocking unauthorized retrieval, detecting watermarks, or filtering out poisoned documents.

sections.heading: 3.1 A Seven-Family Taxonomy of Measured Endpoints
sections.text: We introduce a frozen seven-family taxonomy (Families A, A-pii, and B–F) that groups studies by the exact empirical quantity their primary metric evaluates, rather than where their defense mechanism sits in the RAG pipeline (Table A and Figure 1 ). This design deliberately cuts across the module-based categories used in prior security reviews (§ 4 ). For example, if a paper proposes an unlearning method but evaluates it solely by measuring how often the system refuses to answer forbidden queries, our taxonomy places it under access suppression (Family D) rather than removal. Conversely, if a paper tests whether deleted data can still be reconstructed from residual index states, it belongs to source recovery (Family B). The seven families fall into four broader asset groups based on what is being protected: • Content Disclosure and Formal Proxies (Families A, A-pii, B, and C): These endpoints concern the secrecy of the underlying data. Family A measures whether generated answers copy protected wording verbatim or through close paraphrase. Family A-pii tracks whether the output leaks specific personal identifiers like names or phone numbers. Family B measures whether an attacker can reconstruct source documents outside ordinary text generation, such as by inverting embeddings or inspecting index structures. Family C groups studies that report a mathematical privacy bound (such as differential privacy ε \varepsilon ) or a perplexity shift without measuring actual leaked text. Because Family C reports a theoretical or statistical proxy rather than observed leakage, only Families A, A-pii, and B directly measure content disclosure to a user or adversary. • Access Suppression (Family D): Endpoints here test whether the system blocks unauthorized documents from being retrieved, routed, or used to answer a query, typically through role-based filters or refusal mechanisms. • Corpus-Use Detection (Family E): Rather than preventing data exposure, these endpoints test whether an auditor can prove after the fact that a document or database was used, either by detecting planted watermarks and canaries or by running membership inference audits. • Pipeline Integrity and Attribution (Family F): The largest group in our map evaluates whether the RAG system resists external manipulation (such as corpus poisoning or prompt injection) or correctly attributes generated answers back to their source documents. Family G is reserved for underdetermined cases where the reported packet does not establish a specific technical event. Fixing category boundaries by the measured metric makes cross-paper comparison reproducible. When 32 annotators double-coded all 118 core records using this seven-family scheme, they reached high agreement on the primary endpoint family ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Literature Search, Human Coding, and Corpus Scope
sections.text: To build the evidence map, we searched arXiv, OpenAlex, and the ACL Anthology through July 17, 2026, following standard scoping review protocols ( Tricco et al., 2018 ; Peters et al., 2021 ) . Our queries returned 11,972 total hits, which deduplicated to 8,978 unique records. Screening titles and abstracts narrowed this pool to 925 candidate papers, for which we recovered 824 full texts (Appendix B ). Thirty-two trained annotators with backgrounds in natural language processing, machine learning, security, privacy, and information science double-coded all 824 recoverable full texts. Any disagreements were resolved by an independent adjudicator under a frozen protocol. To verify that our initial screening did not miss relevant work, we also double-screened a stratified sample of 1,200 excluded records to test our stopping rule ( Callaghan et al., 2024 ) . To qualify as a direct RAG-protection study in our core map, a paper had to evaluate a retrieval-augmented system, intervene on its query, corpus, index, context, or output, and report a source-verified protection or attribution metric. Pure attack papers, benchmarks, surveys, and untested proposals were tracked separately, and reporting task utility alone was not enough for inclusion. Each confirmed paper was assigned a single primary endpoint family to prevent multi-module systems from being double-counted as separate studies, while defense mechanisms and intervention stages could receive multiple labels. This process produced 118 full-text-confirmed direct RAG-protection records (112 from the main candidate pool and 6 recovered from the excluded-record audit). For each record, coders annotated 34 structured fields covering system architecture, protected assets, defense mechanisms, measured outcomes, evidence relations, and publication status, reaching a median agreement of κ = 0.94 \kappa=0.94 across all released fields (range 0.56 0.56 to 1.00 1.00 ). We release the de-identified 8,024-row human label matrix alongside verification scripts that recompute agreement across every field (Appendix B ), and we verified every cited operating point directly against the source PDF rather than external metadata (Appendix B.3 ). Our design-based audit of excluded papers estimates that roughly 27.2 additional confirmable studies may exist beyond our candidate pool under the frozen screening rule. Throughout the paper, we report proportions with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals and permutation-test p p -values as exact descriptions of our 118-record analyzed pool, rather than absolute population totals for the entire field (Appendix B.3 ). As we show next, different endpoint families not only measure distinct events, but often move in opposite directions under the very same defense (Table B.3 ).

sections.heading: 4 The Landscape of Defenses by Measured Endpoint
sections.text: Every empirical RAG protection study specifies where it intervenes in the pipeline, what mechanism it applies, and what outcome metric it measures. While prior surveys organize the literature around the first two dimensions ( Mu et al., 2026 ; Palanisamy et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , we organize our analysis around the third. Below, we examine each endpoint family in turn, showing how the defenses tested against it work, where they trade off utility or fail under pressure, and what blind spots their metrics leave behind. All counts refer to the 118 human-coded core records, and Appendix D.2 lists the exact operating points reported by each study.

sections.heading: 4.1 Emitted Text and Identifiers (Families A and A-pii)
sections.text: Families A and A-pii are the only endpoints in our taxonomy that directly score the text a user receives. Family A measures whether the generated response reproduces protected source wording verbatim or through close paraphrase, while Family A-pii tracks whether the response leaks atomic personal identifiers such as names, phone numbers, or email addresses. Despite sitting at the heart of privacy and copyright concerns, these two families together account for just 14 of the 118 records in our map. The defenses evaluated here intervene at four distinct points along the generation path. First, retrieval-side thresholding drops passages whose embedding distance to the query falls outside a safe band, ensuring the generator never sees quotable source text ( Zeng et al., 2024a ) . Second, context transformation rewrites or condenses retrieved passages before generation, using either extractive compression ( Zeng et al., 2025a ) or multi-agent semantic rewriting that paraphrases sensitive spans while keeping the passage useful for answering questions ( Zhao et al., 2027 ) . Third, constrained decoding intervenes during token generation to block verbatim reproduction: privacy-aware decoding adds calibrated noise to next-token probabilities under a differential privacy budget ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , adaptive backtracking rolls the decoder back whenever a partial span begins to match a protected entity ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , and dual-path generation synthesizes answers from a draft model while consulting the protected source only through a restricted reference channel ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Fourth, studies in Family A-pii typically rely on a two-stage filter pair, combining an input judge that blocks extraction-style prompts with an output regular expression or named-entity filter that redacts identifiers before returning the final answer ( Li et al., 2026b ; Moulton et al., 2025 ) . Because emitted-content metrics penalize even partial text overlap, defenses in Families A and A-pii face a much stricter test than binary access checks. As a result, they report the lowest rates of unqualified success across the entire evidence map: 88% of records in Family A and only 50% in Family A-pii report net improvements, compared with 94% to 96% in the access, detection, and integrity families. They are also the two families where adaptive attackers most frequently recover the protected information, occurring in 38% of Family A records and 33% of Family A-pii records, versus just 4% for access suppression, 6% for usage detection, and 0% for pipeline integrity. Looking closely at their operating points explains why achieving complete protection is so difficult. When interventions push text reproduction toward zero, task utility often drops sharply: distance thresholding cuts source copying in Zeng et al. (2024a) at the cost of reducing task ROUGE-L from 0.39 to 0.13, entity-level anonymization can sacrifice up to 35% in Recall@ k k ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and privacy-aware decoding at strict budgets ( ε = 0.01 \varepsilon=0.01 to 0.05 0.05 ) causes model perplexity to diverge ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Conversely, when systems relax these controls to preserve answer quality, noticeable leakage remains. Adaptive backtracking still leaves an average leakage rate (ALR) of 0.13 and a context leakage rate (CLR) of 24.3% ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , while dynamic anonymization leaves residual leakage rates of 0.17 on ChatDoctor and 0.33 on EnronQA ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . Similarly, the multilingual input judge in Li et al. (2026b) blocks English extraction prompts but still leaves 7.5% residual leakage on Arabic queries and 17.5% on Swahili. These divergent numbers show that there is no universal exchange rate between privacy and accuracy in RAG generation. An operating point that looks safe on aggregate copying scores can still fail on specific entity types, non-English queries, or multi-turn extraction prompts. Consequently, studies evaluating Families A and A-pii must report their residual leakage alongside exact workload conditions and utility costs, rather than treating a drop in average text overlap as proof that source content cannot be extracted.

sections.heading: 4.2 Source Reconstruction Outside Generation (Family B)
sections.text: Even if a RAG system never leaks a single word through its generated answers, an attacker can still reconstruct indexed documents through underlying system channels. Family B captures these non-generation reconstruction endpoints, accounting for 7 records in our map (and every record that reports a content-reconstruction metric). Research here targets three distinct leakage channels, each requiring its own defense style. The most widely studied channel is embedding inversion, where an adversary with access to stored vectors runs a trained decoder such as Vec2Text or a fine-tuned T5 model to recover the original text. Defenses against inversion either add entropy-driven perturbations to the vectors ( Jin et al., 2025 ) or apply distance-preserving and homomorphic encryption so the index remains searchable without exposing raw embeddings ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2026 ) . A second channel is index-structure and deletion residue: PRAG demonstrates that a semi-honest server observing HNSW graph traversal paths can reconstruct the underlying document graph without inspecting a single vector ( Li et al., 2026c ) , while Ghost Vectors reveals that soft-deleted embeddings linger in HNSW indices and remain invertible until the index is rebuilt ( Chakraborttii et al., 2026 ) . The third channel is parametric residue, which arises when retrieved knowledge is compressed into distilled LoRA weights rather than passed as text context, turning the adapter weights themselves into an inversion target ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Reversing this threat model, one study treats the vector store as an exfiltration medium and uses outlier detectors to catch steganographically smuggled embeddings ( Wanger, 2026 ) . Interpreting reconstruction scores in Family B requires paying close attention to both the reference object and the strength of the attacker’s decoder. Across the seven studies, defenses measure success against very different targets: distance-preserving encryption drives Vec2Text reconstruction BLEU down from 83 to 12 ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , path-oblivious retrieval cuts HNSW edge recovery from 18.3% to 6.8% alongside a measurable drop in retrieval recall ( Li et al., 2026c ) , and epoch-key rotation reduces ROUGE-L recovery from soft-deleted vectors from 0.207 to 0.000 ( Chakraborttii et al., 2026 ) . Because recovering source wording, graph edges, and deleted vectors are distinct events, these numbers cannot be compared on a single scale. More importantly, a near-zero reconstruction score is only meaningful if the baseline attack actually works on the unprotected system. In the clinical-note experiment of Chakraborttii et al. (2026) , for example, the unprotected baseline yields a Vec2Text ROUGE-L of just 0.009 because the off-the-shelf inverter struggles with domain-specific medical text; in such cases, a low defended score reflects a weak attacker rather than a strong defense. Finally, Family B endpoints are strictly orthogonal to generation endpoints: encrypting embeddings or hiding HNSW traversal paths protects the backend datastore, but it does nothing to stop the language model from quoting retrieved passages verbatim to an end user (Family A).

sections.heading: 4.3 Mathematical Bounds and Likelihood Proxies (Family C)
sections.text: Instead of measuring actual text leakage or document reconstruction, the 6 records in Family C evaluate privacy through theoretical guarantees or statistical proxies, and every record in this family pairs its privacy metric with a task utility score. These studies fall into two distinct groups. The formal sub-family injects calibrated noise into the RAG pipeline and tracks a mathematical privacy budget. Within this group, DP-RDM adapts retrieval-augmented diffusion models to private domains under a differential privacy budget of ε = 10 \varepsilon=10 ( Golatkar et al., 2024 ; Lebensold et al., 2024 ) , while Private-RAG uses individual Rényi privacy filters to answer hundreds of queries at ε ≈ 10 \varepsilon\approx 10 in settings where naive composition would require ε ≈ 1000 \varepsilon\approx 1000 ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . Other formal approaches apply differential privacy directly to token voting during text generation ( Koga et al., 2024 ) or use pure ε \varepsilon -DP SimHash bucketing when building the retrieval datastore ( Abouelenein and Torki, 2026 ) . By contrast, the statistical sub-family measures privacy through changes in model likelihood rather than formal bounds: SILO evaluates nonparametric datastores by comparing the model’s perplexity on a held-out book when related books are present in the index versus when they are removed, treating the likelihood shift itself as the primary endpoint ( Min et al., 2024 ) . While mathematical bounds and likelihood shifts offer clean theoretical targets, they do not measure what a deployed system actually emits to a user, and their numbers cannot be pooled with empirical leakage rates. Even within Family C, reported operating points depend heavily on the protected unit, the composition rule, and the query workload. For example, DP-RDM achieves its ε = 10 \varepsilon=10 guarantee over T = 100 T=100 k queries with a generation FID of 155.67 ( Lebensold et al., 2024 ) , whereas Private-RAG maintains ε ≈ 10 \varepsilon\approx 10 by permanently retiring individual documents from retrieval once their personal privacy budgets are exhausted ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . Meanwhile, the private datastore approach in Abouelenein and Torki (2026) translates its SimHash bucketing guarantee into an empirical audit, reducing membership-inference accuracy from 70.22% to 53.60% at the cost of a 2.6% drop in task accuracy. Because query budgets, neighboring-dataset definitions, and utility trade-offs vary so widely across these setups, a paper reporting ε = 10 \varepsilon=10 and a paper reporting zero verbatim copied spans (Family A) are providing fundamentally different types of evidence, even when evaluated on the exact same corpus.

sections.heading: 4.4 Access and Retrieval Suppression (Family D)
sections.text: Rather than scoring the words in a generated answer, Family D evaluates whether restricted documents are retrieved, routed, or allowed to be answered in the first place. Containing 26 records, this is the largest content-adjacent family in our map, and 96% of its studies report net improvements. Defenses here differ primarily in where they enforce authorization along the pipeline, and their results point to a clear engineering rule: enforcing access checks late in the pipeline is far riskier than enforcing them early. The common retrieve-then-filter pattern, which fetches top- k k passages first and checks permissions afterward, still exposes unauthorized context in 86.1% of base queries ( Namboothiri, 2026 ) . By contrast, pushing authorization down into the database engine through row-level security or predicate pushdown eliminates cross-tenant retrieval leakage entirely ( Budigi and Sirigiri, 2026 ; Arceo and Narsing, 2026 ) . Beyond structural database rules, a second group of defenses relies on semantic or learned policies, filtering passages by inferred user role, governing access at retrieval time, or placing a policy firewall around the RAG pipeline ( Lorenzo et al., 2025 ; Nutakki, 2026 ; Yao et al., 2025a ) . A third group modifies the system architecture or the documents themselves, either isolating the communication channel so raw user prompts never meet protected sources inside the generator ( Cherubin and Paverd, 2025 ) or perturbing source texts so a retrieving model cannot extract usable answers from them ( Agnew et al., 2024 ) . Notably, RAG unlearning studies that measure success by how often the model refuses to answer forbidden questions also fall into Family D rather than a removal category ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . Comparing operating points across Family D highlights a sharp divide between deterministic permission checks and learned semantic filters. When access policies are tied to clean database metadata, engine-level row security drives tenant-isolation leakage from 0.2% down to zero across 1,000 queries ( Budigi and Sirigiri, 2026 ) . However, when permissions must be inferred from natural language or when metadata is imperfect, residual leakage quickly reappears. For example, the AI-driven role filter in ARBITER reaches 85% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.89 over 389 queries, which actually trails the 0.93 to 0.94 F1 achieved by a simple static filter ( Lorenzo et al., 2025 ) . Similarly, hybrid graph-retrieval defenses remain vulnerable when 5% to 10% of document metadata labels are randomly corrupted ( Thornton, 2026a ) , and enterprise confidentiality filters see their recall drop to 74.35% when user queries omit explicit project names ( Byun et al., 2025 ) . More fundamentally, suppressing access or answerability is not the same as preventing content disclosure. On the one hand, a refusal rate measures policy compliance rather than whether sensitive knowledge was truly erased from the system. On the other hand, achieving zero unauthorized retrieval says nothing about what happens when the user is authorized. In commercial or licensed RAG deployments, legitimate subscribers are permitted to retrieve from the datastore, yet the operator must still prevent the model from reproducing copyrighted chapters verbatim. Protecting against that risk requires evaluating emitted expression (Family A) alongside retrieval permissions.

sections.heading: 4.5 Post-Hoc Corpus-Use Detection (Family E)
sections.text: Instead of blocking queries or suppressing generated text, the 18 records in Family E ask a forensic question: can an auditor prove after the fact that a specific document collection was indexed or queried by a RAG system? Strikingly, most studies framed around copyright and dataset ownership concentrate in this family, even though usage detection does not measure or prevent content disclosure. Research here follows four technical paths depending on whether the auditor can modify the corpus beforehand. The dominant design plants a verifiable signal into the data and later probes the suspect system to recover it. Researchers have embedded these signals as statistical watermarks in generated text ( Jovanović et al., 2025 ) , dual-layer semantic and lexical watermarks ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , reasoning traces in chain-of-thought space ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , multi-bit ownership payloads ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , black-box knowledge base watermarks ( Lv et al., 2025 ) , synthetic sentinel documents ( Kwok et al., 2026 ) , retrievability-optimized canaries ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , visual sentinel images ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , and multimodal watermarks for RAG-as-a-Service platforms ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . When planting signals in advance is impossible, a second, signal-free group audits corpus membership directly through black-box queries ( Zeng et al., 2025b ) . Flipping the roles, a third group builds defenses to protect the datastore against membership inference attacks ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) , while a fourth inspects internal model activations or runtime execution games to catch unauthorized extraction ( Zhang et al., 2025c ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . Evaluating Family E endpoints requires separating the reliability of the forensic signal from the secrecy of the underlying text. First, detection scores are highly sensitive to calibration choices, query budgets, the fraction of target material actually indexed, and simple post-processing attacks. For example, the watermark detector in Ward begins to trigger false positives when only 20% of the watermarked document set is present in the target corpus ( Jovanović et al., 2025 ) . Under adversarial paraphrasing, membership audit performance in Zeng et al. (2025b) drops to an AUC of 79.6%. Similarly, applying a detect-and-inpaint filter causes visual sentinel detection to fall from an AUC of 0.99 to 0.62 ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , while injecting external knowledge into the database cuts RAG-WM watermark integrity from 100% down to 46.67% ( Lv et al., 2025 ) . Comparing detectors therefore requires matching their false-positive thresholds and adversarial post-processing budgets. Second, and more fundamentally, a usage detector is an alarm rather than a lock: proving that a document sits inside a remote index says nothing about whether its protected wording was ever emitted to an end user (Family A), nor whether an attacker could reconstruct that wording without triggering the alarm.

sections.heading: 4.6 Pipeline Integrity, Attribution, and Recurring Failure Modes (Family F)
sections.text: Accounting for 47 records (40% of our entire map), Family F is by far the largest endpoint category, covering defenses against corpus poisoning, prompt injection, and provenance failures. Rather than protecting the secrecy of indexed documents, these endpoints test whether the RAG pipeline returns trustworthy, uncorrupted answers and correctly credits its sources. Poisoning defenses intervene at three stages of the pipeline. Admission-time filters screen out malicious documents before they enter the index using perplexity scores, Mahalanobis distance, vector hubness, or inter-document similarity ( Cheng et al., 2025b ; Xian et al., 2024 ; Pathak and Sharma, 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . Retrieval-time defenses re-rank candidate passages, partition the retrieved set, or analyze context structure to isolate corrupted chunks ( Pathmanathan et al., 2025 ; Saxena et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2025b ) . Generation-time defenses aggregate answers across multiple passages, sometimes providing formal robustness certificates under a bounded poisoning budget, or isolate untrusted spans during synthesis ( Tan et al., 2026 ; Sharma, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Alongside poisoning defenses, prompt-injection studies enforce runtime control-flow integrity or deploy layered input scanners ( Saleem et al., 2026 ; Alam et al., 2026 ) , while a separate attribution literature traces poisoned outputs back to responsible documents, localizes corrupted spans at the character level, or uses internal model states to verify answer provenance ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Cui and Liu, 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Qi et al., 2024 ) . Comparing evaluation practices in Family F against the rest of the map reveals a telling contrast. Because poisoning and injection studies draw heavily from adversarial machine learning, 51% of Family F records receive a low-concern rating for adaptive robustness testing, and 45% explicitly document an adaptive attack among their failure modes. For example, while a non-adaptive guardrail reports a true-positive rate of 1.000 at a false-positive rate of 0.015 ( Cohen et al., 2024 ) , adaptive white-box attacks like PoisonedRAG-W push document-detector false-negative rates up to roughly 96% ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , and consistency collusion bypasses 70.3% of multi-agent audits ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Yet despite this strong tradition of adaptive testing, zero records in Family F document an attacker recovering protected source content against the proposed defense. The reason is simple: in Family F, an attack success rate (ASR) measures whether the attacker tricked the system into outputting a targeted wrong answer, executing a hijacked instruction, or citing the wrong source. Keeping ASR at zero guarantees that the pipeline behaves as the operator intended, but it is completely compatible with a system that answers every user query by quoting its private or copyrighted sources verbatim. Looking across all seven endpoint families (Families A, A-pii, and B–F), three recurring evaluation patterns explain why reported operating points rarely transfer from one setting to another (Appendix D ). First, defenses face steep protection-utility trade-offs whose magnitudes are seldom reported on a shared scale ( Zeng et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Second, claims of zero residual leakage almost always depend on fragile assumptions, such as perfectly clean permission metadata or attackers who explicitly name their target entities in the query ( Nutakki, 2026 ; Chakraborttii et al., 2026 ) . Third, moving from static queries to adaptive attackers routinely overturns the apparent success of a defense ( Yao et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) . These recurring limitations point to deeper structural gaps in how RAG protection is designed and evaluated, which we audit next.

sections.heading: 5 Three Blind Spots in RAG Protection Research
sections.text: Stepping back from individual endpoint families, our evidence map allows us to audit how the RAG protection literature as a whole connects methods, claims, and evaluations. Reading the 118 human-coded studies across families exposes three systemic blind spots that explain why progress in this field is so difficult to compare.

sections.heading: 5.1 Blind Spot I: Mechanisms Do Not Dictate Endpoints
sections.text: When readers encounter a RAG defense that “reranks retrieved passages” or “rewrites context before generation,” they naturally assume the mechanism tells them what risk is being mitigated. To test this assumption, we cross-tabulated the 13 coded defense mechanism types against the primary endpoint family each paper actually measured (Appendix D ). While mechanism type and endpoint family are statistically associated (mutual information of 0.624 bits versus 0.211 bits under 20,000 label permutations, p = 5 × 10 − 5 p=5\times 10^{-5} ), the link is surprisingly weak. Knowing a paper’s defense mechanisms accounts for only 27% of the uncertainty in its endpoint distribution. In fact, a leave-one-out classifier that sees a paper’s entire set of defense mechanisms predicts its measured endpoint family only 53.4% of the time, barely outperforming the 39.8% baseline of always guessing Family F. Only two specialized mechanisms point reliably to a single endpoint: poisoning and integrity controls are evaluated on an integrity endpoint (Family F) in 94% of their records, and watermarking techniques are evaluated on usage detection (Family E) in 92%. For every other mechanism in the literature, the modal endpoint family accounts for just 28% to 68% of records. This dispersion is most striking for the two most popular interventions in our map: retrieval reranking or thresholding (40 records) and context transformation or summarization (39 records), which span five and six of the seven endpoint families, respectively. In practice, the exact same technical intervention, such as rewriting retrieved passages before they reach the generator, is presented as a verbatim-copying defense in one paper, a PII redaction tool in a second, an access-control filter in a third, and a poisoning defense in a fourth, scored on a completely different endpoint each time. Relying on high-level metric names is almost as ambiguous as relying on mechanism names (Appendix D ). Only a handful of specialized metrics identify the underlying protection event on their own: content-reconstruction scores (7 records) appear exclusively in Family B, attribution metrics appear only in Family F, and literal text-overlap scores concentrate in Families A and A-pii (14 records). By contrast, task utility appears across 58 records (49%) spanning every single family, and attack success rate (ASR) or integrity metrics appear in 61 records across multiple families, making ASR the single most common metric in our map. Because a low ASR can mean anything from blocked prompt injection to failed PII extraction, neither a paper’s architectural mechanism nor its headline metric label reliably tells a reader what asset was actually protected.

sections.heading: 5.2 Blind Spot II: High-Stakes Claims vs. Skipped Content Disclosure
sections.text: When we organize the literature by what it actually measures rather than what mechanisms it uses, a massive gap appears where direct content protection should be. Across our 118 human-coded records, only 21 studies (17.8%) have their primary endpoint in Families A, A-pii, or B, which scores what a user receives or what an attacker can reconstruct from the system. Even if we include mathematical bounds and likelihood proxies from Family C, 77.1% of the literature (91 records in Families D, E, and F) has its primary endpoint outside this broader group. Although document takedown, copyright opt-out, and the right to erasure are among the most concrete demands placed on real-world RAG operators, papers addressing those topics evaluate their methods through text-overlap scores, reconstruction proxies, or query refusal rates, landing in Families A, B, C, or D rather than demonstrating actual source removal. This skew is especially pronounced in research framed around copyright and dataset ownership. Among the 15 records coded with the frozen direct copyright or ownership evidence relation, 11 (73.3% [48.0, 89.1]) have a usage-detection primary endpoint in Family E, compared with just 7 of the 103 records (6.8%) addressing neighboring security or privacy goals (Bonferroni-adjusted p = 4.9 × 10 − 7 p=4.9\times 10^{-7} across 14 comparisons). Meanwhile, zero records under this frozen label have a strict emitted-expression primary endpoint in Family A (95% exact upper bound of 18.1%). This coded subset overwhelmingly prioritizes post-hoc corpus-use detection, leaving verbatim reproduction by the generator absent from its primary endpoints.

sections.heading: 5.3 Blind Spot III: Toy Benchmarks and Static Adversaries
sections.text: Even when a paper selects a clear endpoint that matches its claim, the strength of its evidence depends on the corpus, the adversary, and the rigor of the experimental protocol. Across our map, 112 of the 118 records name a specific evaluation dataset, spanning 278 distinct corpora in total (Appendix D ). Yet the literature relies overwhelmingly on standard open-domain question-answering benchmarks rather than datasets designed to test data protection. The three most popular corpora are Natural Questions (35 records), HotpotQA (31), and MS MARCO (28), followed at a distance by TriviaQA (7) and PopQA (5). By contrast, datasets containing genuinely sensitive or private records appear far less often, led by the Enron Email corpus (12 records), HealthCareMagic (6), and ChatDoctor (5). Evaluating privacy or copyright defenses on general encyclopedia and web-search passages creates an obvious interpretation problem: because these corpora contain little sensitive or proprietary expression to begin with, a low measured leakage rate may simply reflect a benign workload rather than an effective defense. A similar concentration appears in model and retriever choices, where evaluations cluster around GPT-4o (31 records), GPT-4o-mini (20), Contriever (18), all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (12), GPT-3.5 (12), Mistral-7B (12), Llama-3.1-8B (12), and Qwen2.5-7B (11). Sharing a generator or retriever across papers does not make their protection numbers comparable if one study scores corpus membership on Wikipedia while another scores verbatim copying on clinical notes. Threat models and adversary interaction budgets are equally narrow. Across the 118 studies, 47 assume an external black-box attacker and 39 model a malicious corpus contributor with write access, alongside 13 that assume a white-box system operator and 6 that treat a cloud service provider as a protocol participant (with 110 of 118 studies focusing exclusively on text). Only 16 records model an authorized user, even though licensed knowledge bases face their greatest extraction risk from legitimate subscribers who are permitted to query the system but prohibited from copying the underlying database verbatim. Worse still, most interactive evaluations restrict the adversary to a static, one-shot interaction. Fifty-one records allow the attacker only a single query and 25 model no interactive querying at all, whereas just 11 studies grant the adversary feedback-adaptive multi-query access. Testing a defense against a single fixed prompt provides little assurance against a real-world user who can inspect the system’s initial reply and iteratively refine follow-up queries to bypass filters. These gentle evaluation conditions help explain why reported outcomes in the literature are so uniformly positive. In our eight-domain methodological appraisal (Appendix D ), zero records raise high concern regarding threat-model definition or artifact availability, and 95% receive low concern for comparator and ablation design. However, only 48 of 118 records receive low concern for adaptive robustness testing, 72 records (61%) raise high concern for uncertainty analysis because they report single point estimates without confidence intervals, random-seed variance, or statistical tests, and 109 records raise some concern for evaluation independence (with only one record achieving low concern) because defenses are almost always tested by their own authors against locally implemented attacks. Against this backdrop, 108 of the 118 records (92%) report that their proposed intervention improves protection, compared with just 9 reporting mixed effects and 1 reporting net degradation. This 92% success rate should not be read as proof that RAG protection is largely solved; rather, it reflects a literature that predominantly tests self-implemented defenses against non-adaptive attackers on general-purpose QA benchmarks, without quantifying statistical uncertainty.

sections.heading: 6 Controlled Testbed and Future Directions
sections.text: Our literature audit shows that RAG protection studies rarely make content disclosure their primary endpoint, rely heavily on non-adaptive attackers, and use metrics that cannot be compared across families. To demonstrate why these distinctions matter in practice, we first present results from a controlled experimental testbed that evaluates multiple defenses across competing endpoints on the exact same workload, and then outline three priorities for future research.

sections.heading: 6.1 Stopping Surface Copying Does Not Stop Fact Recovery
sections.text: To test whether a defense that succeeds on one endpoint actually protects underlying content on another, we built a controlled evaluation testbed spanning 192 documents across two domains (Wikipedia and scientific papers) and two access policies, paired with three unexposed human-authored fact probes per document and 64 document-disjoint utility queries (full protocol and tables in Appendix C ). Fixing dense retrieval at MiniLM top-3 and greedy decoding, we evaluated four representative controls across Qwen3-8B (primary), Phi-4-14B (replication), Qwen2.5-3B, and Mistral-7B: pre-generation access policy filtering (Family D), a cosine similarity threshold at 0.5 (Family D), an upstream summarization prompt instructing the model to answer in its own words (Family A), and a normalized 8-gram output guard that redacts spans matching protected-source 8-grams while retaining unmatched text (Family A). Crucially, rather than scoring a single static prompt, we also evaluated an online three-query adaptive controller that observes released text, refusals, and redactions to iteratively extract information. Evaluating these defenses simultaneously across multiple endpoints confirms our central thesis: eliminating surface copying does not prevent an attacker from recovering private facts or identifying source documents (Tables C.2 , C.2 , and C.2 ). On quotation-denied items, uncontrolled models copy 20-token source spans verbatim ( copy 20 ) at high rates, reaching 64.1% to 89.1% under natural dense retrieval and up to 96.9% under separator-evasion attacks. Adding the normalized 8-gram guard drives both visible and decoded copy 20 down to 0.0% [0.0, 0.0] in the three-query adaptive evaluation. Yet when we score the exact same guarded responses on fact recovery and source linkage, substantial disclosure remains. Under the three-query adaptive budget, an attacker facing the normalized guard still recovers 48.3% [36.7, 60.8] of hidden source facts on Qwen3-8B (31.7% on Qwen2.5-3B) and links the response back to the exact source document ( re-ID@1 ) 42.5% of the time (Table C.2 ). Blinded human annotations of 192 source-response pairs ( κ = 0.831 \kappa=0.831 for expression, κ = 0.929 \kappa=0.929 for recovery; Table C.3 ) tell the same story: on Phi-4-14B, the normalized guard reduces human-judged substantial content recovery only from 66.7% to 38.9% (Table C.2 ). Furthermore, query budget sensitivity exposes the danger of one-shot testing: on guarded Qwen3-8B, hidden-fact recall is just 3.3% [0.0, 7.5] after a single query, but jumps to 48.3% on the third adaptive turn (Table C.2 ). Our testbed also shows how easily endpoint and metric choices can distort comparisons of prompt-based defenses and task utility. In our single planned confirmatory contrast on 80 held-out answer-only items, the upstream Summary defense yields a difference-in-differences (DiD) in context-attributable exact-answer recall of just − 0.4 -0.4 percentage points [ − 8.3 -8.3 , 7.5 7.5 ] on Qwen3-8B and 0.0 0.0 [ − 7.9 -7.9 , 8.3 8.3 ] on Phi-4-14B (Figure C.4 ). Short exact-answer recall has only 51.8% sensitivity against human-judged recovery and correlates with response length (Table C.3 ). Response length also confounds standard utility metrics: while the Summary prompt appears to hurt ordinary-QA token F1 by − 4.0 -4.0 to − 7.9 -7.9 points across models (Figure C.4 ), our format diagnostic reveals that token F1 heavily penalizes verbose free-form answers (scoring 18.9 on Qwen3-8B versus 46.8 when prompted for short answers; Table C.4 ). Finally, structural access controls fail in complementary ways: pre-retrieval policy filtering blocks unauthorized documents when metadata is clean, but a 12.5% rate of missing metadata labels under a fail-open policy immediately restores 9.4% to 12.5% verbatim copying (Table C.2 ). Across every layer of the pipeline, a defense is only as strong as the specific endpoint, query budget, and metadata assumptions under which it is tested.

sections.heading: 6.2 Three Golden Rules for Future RAG Protection
sections.text: Together, our evidence map and controlled testbed point to three concrete rules for designing, reporting, and reviewing future RAG protection studies. First, studies whose claims concern data secrecy, privacy, or copyright must measure content disclosure directly. In our human-coded map, 97 of the 118 core records do not use content disclosure as their primary endpoint, and most evaluations rely on general-purpose question-answering benchmarks that contain little sensitive text to begin with (§ 5.3 ). Suppressing retrieval access (Family D), detecting watermarks after the fact (Family E), and blocking poisoned passages (Family F) are valuable operational goals, but they do not replace a measurement of what the system actually leaks to a user. Any defense claiming to protect the contents of a retrieval corpus should pair its operational metric with a direct disclosure endpoint from Family A, A-pii, or B, and evaluate on corpora containing genuinely sensitive or proprietary spans. Second, authors and benchmarks should state their target endpoint at subfamily resolution and test against multi-turn, adaptive adversaries. Naming the exact evidenced cell among our 17 subfamilies (for example, distinguishing A.verbatim from A.near , or D.retrieve from D.answer ) allows readers and meta-analyses to compare papers at a stated level of detail without pooling incompatible metrics. Likewise, because single-query evaluations routinely miss extraction vulnerabilities that emerge over three or more adaptive turns (§ 6.1 ), multi-query feedback-adaptive testing and imperfect metadata stress tests should become standard practice rather than rare exceptions. Third, the field must move beyond simple event matching to validate evidential sufficiency. Our taxonomy establishes which technical event a paper measures, not whether the chosen metric is a sufficient or unbiased measure of that event. True evidential sufficiency requires convergent and discriminant validity controls ( Campbell and Fiske, 1959 ) that almost no RAG protection study currently reports. In practice, this means verifying that an extraction or inversion attack is genuinely strong on the unprotected baseline before claiming credit for a low defended score, and checking that utility metrics like token F1 are not confounded by simple shifts in response length.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: “Protection” in retrieval-augmented generation is not a single event. By introducing a frozen seven-family endpoint taxonomy and coordinating 32 annotators to double-code 118 full-text RAG protection studies ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ), we showed that the literature evaluates fundamentally different technical outcomes that cannot be pooled or treated as interchangeable. Looking across this evidence map reveals that defense mechanisms weakly predict what is actually measured, that only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary endpoint, and that evaluations overwhelmingly rely on benign question-answering benchmarks and non-adaptive adversaries. Our controlled testbed confirms the practical stakes of these distinctions: defenses that eliminate verbatim span copying still leave substantial source facts recoverable under multi-turn adaptive querying. By releasing our human-coded evidence map, taxonomy protocols, and evaluation testbed, we aim to help the community move from ambiguous umbrella claims toward precise, comparable, and construct-valid evaluations within each protection goal.

sections.heading: Appendix A Event and Control Schema
sections.text: To prevent our coding from confusing a paper’s high-level topic with what its experiments actually measure, our schema records six dimensions separately: the technical event, the protected asset, the adversary’s identity and access level, the defensive intervention function, the primary measured endpoint, and the broader evidence relation (Table A a). Table A b defines our frozen seven-family endpoint taxonomy (Families A, A-pii, and B–F). Families A, A-pii, B, and C are grouped under the shared content-secrecy asset class; however, when we count studies whose primary endpoint measures actual content disclosure, we include only Families A, A-pii, and B because Family C reports theoretical bounds or likelihood shifts without observing emitted or reconstructed text. Under this four-group hierarchy, a paper’s claim and its primary measured endpoint are coded as concordant when they fall into the exact same family, partial when they land in different families within the same asset group, and discordant (off-target) when they belong to different asset groups altogether. Family G is assigned whenever a claim or an experimental packet is too vague to establish a specific technical event. Finally, each publication receives a single mutually exclusive primary endpoint family from human adjudication, whereas its defense mechanisms and intervention functions can receive multiple labels. sections.heading: B.1 Literature Search and Eligibility Criteria
sections.text: Our literature search ran through July 17, 2026, combining eight initial arXiv queries, nine expanded arXiv query families, the same nine query families executed over OpenAlex, and a title-and-metadata scan of the ACL Anthology. We also ran ten seed-paper lookups and ten forward-citation tracking passes as separate continuity checks, alongside capped supplementary searches on Crossref and DBLP. Each search family paired core retrieval terms (such as “RAG,” “retrieval-augmented,” “retrieval-enhanced,” and “grounded generation”) with protection-related keywords covering copyright, licensing, ownership, watermarking, copying, extraction, privacy, attribution, removal, and security; an adjacent query family paired general language-model terms with copyright and copying prevention. Retrieved records were deduplicated sequentially by arXiv identifier, Digital Object Identifier (DOI), and normalized title, followed by an author-title-year audit that linked multiple preprints or versions belonging to the same underlying study. To be confirmed as a direct empirical RAG-protection record in our core map, a study had to evaluate a retrieval-augmented system, intervene on its query, corpus, index, context, or output, report a source-verified protection or attribution operating point, and address either a direct copyright/ownership goal or a neighboring RAG privacy/security goal. Pure attack papers, standalone benchmarks, survey articles, and untested architectural proposals were tracked in separate roles, and reporting task utility alone was not sufficient for inclusion. In total, our queries returned 11,972 raw hits, which deduplicated to 8,978 unique records and yielded 925 candidate inclusions after abstract screening. We successfully recovered full texts for 824 candidates, while 101 full texts were unavailable and one recovered paper remained unresolved. Human full-text review confirmed 112 direct control studies from this candidate pool, and our stratified audit of 1,200 records sampled from the 8,053 excluded records identified 6 additional direct controls, bringing the final human-coded map to 118 records (Table B.1 a and Table B.1 b). sections.heading: B.2 Human Annotation and Inter-Rater Reliability
sections.text: Thirty-two trained annotators with backgrounds in NLP and machine learning (18), security and privacy (9), and information science or law and technology (5) double-coded the recovered full texts. Whenever the initial pair disagreed, a third reviewer outside that pair adjudicated the record. Before coding the main pool, every annotator completed a 100-item calibration test with a required passing score of 95%; all 32 annotators passed, scoring between 95% and 98% (median 97%). Because raw calibration files and identity-linked records remain restricted under participant confidentiality terms, domain backgrounds and calibration pass rates are reported as coordinator attestations. Our public artifact releases a de-identified 8,024-row human label matrix covering all 118 confirmed records across 34 coded fields. In this matrix, initial coder pairs that had no entry in the disagreement log are reconstructed as matching the consensus label, while logged disagreements preserve the exact pre-adjudication calls of both coders. Running our standalone verification script on this matrix reproduces a pre-adjudication agreement of 89.83% ( κ = 0.8672 \kappa=0.8672 ) on the primary endpoint family (Table B.2 a and Table B.2 b). Across the 14 strictly categorical fields, median reliability is κ = 0.87 \kappa=0.87 . Fifteen free-text rationale and source-location fields had no logged categorical disagreements; their nominal κ = 1.00 \kappa=1.00 reflects consensus text entry rather than an independent reliability estimate. sections.heading: C.1 Design and analysis hierarchy
sections.text: The fixed protocol (not preregistered) uses a 192-document security corpus across two domains and two policies, with three unexposed human-authored probes per document; utility uses 64 document-disjoint open-policy items. MiniLM dense retrieval is fixed at top-3, decoding is greedy, and the three-query controller observes only released text, redaction, refusal, transport decodability, and released length. Qwen3 is the primary model, Phi-4 the replication, and Qwen2.5-3B and Mistral-7B exploratory. The exact upstream Summary baseline is commit-pinned. The sole planned confirmatory contrast is the Qwen3 Summary-minus-uncontrolled difference-in-differences (DiD) of exact hidden-probe recall on all 80 held-out answer-only items. Context effects are target-present minus target-ablated. An attack ranking selected on uncontrolled target-present development data is shared across all four exposure/control cells. Inference uses paired source-item bootstrapping and sign randomisation without multiplicity correction for this single contrast. Yet RAG protection studies use incompatible evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models. We present a systematic survey and human-coded evidence map of 118 full-text-confirmed RAG defense papers, organized by measured endpoint rather than claimed goal or defense mechanism. Our seven-family taxonomy covers content disclosure, formal privacy proxies, access control and suppression, corpus-use detection, and pipeline integrity and attribution. Thirty-two annotators double-coded the papers ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ). The survey identifies three gaps. First, retrieval reranking and context rewriting each span five or six endpoint families, so mechanisms do not identify protection outcomes. Second, only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary endpoint; under the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% of records have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, and none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, most evaluations use general-purpose question-answering datasets and non-adaptive attacks rather than sensitive data and adaptive, multi-turn extraction. Our controlled RAG testbed shows that preventing verbatim copying does not prevent private-fact recovery: a normalized 8-gram guard reduces 20-token copying to 0.0%, but a three-query adaptive attacker recovers 48.3% of hidden facts on Qwen3-8B. We release the taxonomy, dataset, coding protocols, and testbed to enable comparable, claim-aligned RAG security evaluation. 1 Introduction Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects language models to external document collections at inference time ( Lewis et al., 2020 ; Gao, 2023 ) . Because this external datastore can be searched, updated, and quoted directly, it creates new risks around privacy, copyright, and system security. Even if a document never appeared in pre-training, a RAG system might still leak its private details, copy its wording verbatim, or fall victim to poisoned entries. A rapidly growing literature aims to “protect” RAG systems against these risks, yet papers using this label rarely measure the same thing. Consider two studies that both claim to protect the copyright of a retrieval database. The first plants a watermark to prove after the fact that the database was queried, while the second blocks unauthorized users from retrieving restricted documents. A third study defends against poisoned passages to keep answers accurate, and a fourth rewrites retrieved text so the generator cannot copy it word for word. All four papers report successful “protection,” but they evaluate completely different technical events. Treating them as interchangeable, or pooling their scores to compare defenses, is like comparing a burglar alarm to a fireproof safe. Existing surveys organize this literature by threat model, pipeline stage, or system architecture. However, knowing where a defense sits in the pipeline tells us very little about what it actually achieves. In this work, we take a different approach: we survey RAG protection research based on the exact empirical endpoint each study measures. We define a frozen seven-family taxonomy of measured endpoints (Table A and Figure 1 ) that separates actual content disclosure from access control, usage detection, and pipeline integrity. Using this taxonomy, 32 annotators double-coded 118 full-text-confirmed RAG protection papers, reaching high agreement on what each paper measures ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ). Looking at the literature through its measured endpoints reveals three major blind spots. First, defense mechanisms only weakly predict what a paper tests (§ 5.1 ). Popular techniques such as retrieval reranking and context rewriting are evaluated across five or six different endpoint families, meaning readers cannot infer what was protected just from how the system was built. Second, research attention is heavily skewed away from actual data leakage (§ 5 ). Only 21 of the 118 papers (17.8%) have a primary endpoint that measures whether protected content is emitted to the user or reconstructed from the system. Among studies with the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, whereas none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, evaluation setups often fail to stress-test the defenses they propose (§ 5.3 ). Most studies rely on standard question-answering datasets that contain little sensitive content to begin with, and very few test against adaptive attackers who can ask follow-up questions. Our own controlled experiments confirm why this distinction matters: defenses that drive word-for-word copying down to zero still allow attackers to recover the underlying private facts (Appendix C ). To help future work build on clear empirical foundations, we make four contributions: • An endpoint-based survey that organizes RAG defense mechanisms, evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models by the exact technical event they measure (§ 4 , § 5.3 ). • A validated seven-family event taxonomy that makes cross-paper comparisons reproducible (§ 3 ). • A human-coded evidence map of 118 direct RAG protection papers, complete with item-level annotations, operating points, and open-source verification tools (§ 3 , Appendix D.2 ). • A critical audit and controlled testbed examining reporting quality, and the gap between stopping surface copying and preventing fact recovery (§ 5 , § 6 , Appendix C ). 2 Related Work Prior surveys of RAG security and privacy organize the field around system architecture and attack surfaces. Broad reviews of language model privacy cover threats like membership inference and data poisoning ( Das et al., 2025 ) alongside cryptographic and differentially private defenses ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . Dedicated surveys on copyright and ownership focus on text and model watermarking ( Yang et al., 2025 ) or fingerprinting techniques ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Within the RAG literature specifically, existing reviews group studies by threat model, pipeline stage, or defensive module ( Mu et al., 2026 ; Palanisamy et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . While this architectural view shows where a defense intervenes, it obscures what the evaluation actually tests. Individual empirical studies already hint at this divergence: papers evaluating literal and non-literal text reproduction ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , copyright-sensitive activation steering ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , proprietary knowledge base defense ( Li et al., 2026a ) , and knowledge extraction benchmarks ( Qi et al., 2026 ) all define “protection” through different operational outcomes. Furthermore, recent adaptation methods train models to decide when to retrieve, critique context, or withhold answers ( Asai et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) , blurring the boundary between parametric memory and external datastores. Rather than grouping papers by where their mechanisms sit in the pipeline, we human-code the exact technical events their experiments measure. Our approach builds on meta-scientific audits of machine learning research ( Lipton and Steinhardt, 2019 ; Kapoor and Narayanan, 2023 ) and classical measurement theory, which requires clearly defining target concepts and validating how they are measured ( Cronbach and Meehl, 1955 ; Campbell and Fiske, 1959 ; Messick, 1995 ) . These principles have shaped recent critiques of benchmark design and fairness evaluation in natural language processing ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ; Blodgett et al., 2021 ; Raji et al., 2021 ; Bowman and Dahl, 2021 ) . However, while prior audits typically expose flaws inside an experimental setup, we examine the link between two separate components of a paper: its high-level protection claim and its measured empirical endpoint. This focus on claim-measurement alignment parallels recent findings in question answering, where standard lexical overlap metrics often fail to capture true semantic accuracy ( Bulian et al., 2022 ; Kamalloo et al., 2023 ; Adlakha et al., 2024 ) .
