A record is assigned by its primary measured endpoint, not by its topic. 3 The Endpoint Taxonomy and Human-Coded Evidence Map To compare RAG protection studies fairly, we first need a clear way to categorize what their experiments actually measure. Treating “protection” as a single outcome confuses very different technical events. Stopping a model from copying source text word for word is not the same as hiding personal identifiers, preventing attackers from inverting vector embeddings, proving a differential privacy bound, blocking unauthorized retrieval, detecting watermarks, or filtering out poisoned documents. 3.1 A Seven-Family Taxonomy of Measured Endpoints We introduce a frozen seven-family taxonomy (Families A, A-pii, and B–F) that groups studies by the exact empirical quantity their primary metric evaluates, rather than where their defense mechanism sits in the RAG pipeline (Table A and Figure 1 ). This design deliberately cuts across the module-based categories used in prior security reviews (§ 4 ). For example, if a paper proposes an unlearning method but evaluates it solely by measuring how often the system refuses to answer forbidden queries, our taxonomy places it under access suppression (Family D) rather than removal. Conversely, if a paper tests whether deleted data can still be reconstructed from residual index states, it belongs to source recovery (Family B). The seven families fall into four broader asset groups based on what is being protected: • Content Disclosure and Formal Proxies (Families A, A-pii, B, and C): These endpoints concern the secrecy of the underlying data. Family A measures whether generated answers copy protected wording verbatim or through close paraphrase. Family A-pii tracks whether the output leaks specific personal identifiers like names or phone numbers. Family B measures whether an attacker can reconstruct source documents outside ordinary text generation, such as by inverting embeddings or inspecting index structures. Family C groups studies that report a mathematical privacy bound (such as differential privacy ε \varepsilon ) or a perplexity shift without measuring actual leaked text. Because Family C reports a theoretical or statistical proxy rather than observed leakage, only Families A, A-pii, and B directly measure content disclosure to a user or adversary. • Access Suppression (Family D): Endpoints here test whether the system blocks unauthorized documents from being retrieved, routed, or used to answer a query, typically through role-based filters or refusal mechanisms. • Corpus-Use Detection (Family E): Rather than preventing data exposure, these endpoints test whether an auditor can prove after the fact that a document or database was used, either by detecting planted watermarks and canaries or by running membership inference audits. • Pipeline Integrity and Attribution (Family F): The largest group in our map evaluates whether the RAG system resists external manipulation (such as corpus poisoning or prompt injection) or correctly attributes generated answers back to their source documents. Family G is reserved for underdetermined cases where the reported packet does not establish a specific technical event. Fixing category boundaries by the measured metric makes cross-paper comparison reproducible. When 32 annotators double-coded all 118 core records using this seven-family scheme, they reached high agreement on the primary endpoint family ( κ = 0.867 \kappa=0.867 ). 3.2 Literature Search, Human Coding, and Corpus Scope To build the evidence map, we searched arXiv, OpenAlex, and the ACL Anthology through July 17, 2026, following standard scoping review protocols ( Tricco et al., 2018 ; Peters et al., 2021 ) . Our queries returned 11,972 total hits, which deduplicated to 8,978 unique records. Screening titles and abstracts narrowed this pool to 925 candidate papers, for which we recovered 824 full texts (Appendix B ). Thirty-two trained annotators with backgrounds in natural language processing, machine learning, security, privacy, and information science double-coded all 824 recoverable full texts. Any disagreements were resolved by an independent adjudicator under a frozen protocol. To verify that our initial screening did not miss relevant work, we also double-screened a stratified sample of 1,200 excluded records to test our stopping rule ( Callaghan et al., 2024 ) . To qualify as a direct RAG-protection study in our core map, a paper had to evaluate a retrieval-augmented system, intervene on its query, corpus, index, context, or output, and report a source-verified protection or attribution metric. Pure attack papers, benchmarks, surveys, and untested proposals were tracked separately, and reporting task utility alone was not enough for inclusion. Each confirmed paper was assigned a single primary endpoint family to prevent multi-module systems from being double-counted as separate studies, while defense mechanisms and intervention stages could receive multiple labels. This process produced 118 full-text-confirmed direct RAG-protection records (112 from the main candidate pool and 6 recovered from the excluded-record audit). For each record, coders annotated 34 structured fields covering system architecture, protected assets, defense mechanisms, measured outcomes, evidence relations, and publication status, reaching a median agreement of κ = 0.94 \kappa=0.94 across all released fields (range 0.56 0.56 to 1.00 1.00 ). We release the de-identified 8,024-row human label matrix alongside verification scripts that recompute agreement across every field (Appendix B ), and we verified every cited operating point directly against the source PDF rather than external metadata (Appendix B.3 ). Our design-based audit of excluded papers estimates that roughly 27.2 additional confirmable studies may exist beyond our candidate pool under the frozen screening rule. Throughout the paper, we report proportions with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals and permutation-test p p -values as exact descriptions of our 118-record analyzed pool, rather than absolute population totals for the entire field (Appendix B.3 ). As we show next, different endpoint families not only measure distinct events, but often move in opposite directions under the very same defense (Table B.3 ). 4 The Landscape of Defenses by Measured Endpoint Every empirical RAG protection study specifies where it intervenes in the pipeline, what mechanism it applies, and what outcome metric it measures. While prior surveys organize the literature around the first two dimensions ( Mu et al., 2026 ; Palanisamy et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , we organize our analysis around the third. Below, we examine each endpoint family in turn, showing how the defenses tested against it work, where they trade off utility or fail under pressure, and what blind spots their metrics leave behind. All counts refer to the 118 human-coded core records, and Appendix D.2 lists the exact operating points reported by each study. 4.1 Emitted Text and Identifiers (Families A and A-pii) Families A and A-pii are the only endpoints in our taxonomy that directly score the text a user receives. Family A measures whether the generated response reproduces protected source wording verbatim or through close paraphrase, while Family A-pii tracks whether the response leaks atomic personal identifiers such as names, phone numbers, or email addresses. Despite sitting at the heart of privacy and copyright concerns, these two families together account for just 14 of the 118 records in our map. The defenses evaluated here intervene at four distinct points along the generation path. First, retrieval-side thresholding drops passages whose embedding distance to the query falls outside a safe band, ensuring the generator never sees quotable source text ( Zeng et al., 2024a ) . Second, context transformation rewrites or condenses retrieved passages before generation, using either extractive compression ( Zeng et al., 2025a ) or multi-agent semantic rewriting that paraphrases sensitive spans while keeping the passage useful for answering questions ( Zhao et al., 2027 ) . Third, constrained decoding intervenes during token generation to block verbatim reproduction: privacy-aware decoding adds calibrated noise to next-token probabilities under a differential privacy budget ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , adaptive backtracking rolls the decoder back whenever a partial span begins to match a protected entity ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , and dual-path generation synthesizes answers from a draft model while consulting the protected source only through a restricted reference channel ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Fourth, studies in Family A-pii typically rely on a two-stage filter pair, combining an input judge that blocks extraction-style prompts with an output regular expression or named-entity filter that redacts identifiers before returning the final answer ( Li et al., 2026b ; Moulton et al., 2025 ) . Because emitted-content metrics penalize even partial text overlap, defenses in Families A and A-pii face a much stricter test than binary access checks. As a result, they report the lowest rates of unqualified success across the entire evidence map: 88% of records in Family A and only 50% in Family A-pii report net improvements, compared with 94% to 96% in the access, detection, and integrity families. They are also the two families where adaptive attackers most frequently recover the protected information, occurring in 38% of Family A records and 33% of Family A-pii records, versus just 4% for access suppression, 6% for usage detection, and 0% for pipeline integrity. Looking closely at their operating points explains why achieving complete protection is so difficult. When interventions push text reproduction toward zero, task utility often drops sharply: distance thresholding cuts source copying in Zeng et al. (2024a) at the cost of reducing task ROUGE-L from 0.39 to 0.13, entity-level anonymization can sacrifice up to 35% in Recall@ k k ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and privacy-aware decoding at strict budgets ( ε = 0.01 \varepsilon=0.01 to 0.05 0.05 ) causes model perplexity to diverge ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Conversely, when systems relax these controls to preserve answer quality, noticeable leakage remains. Adaptive backtracking still leaves an average leakage rate (ALR) of 0.13 and a context leakage rate (CLR) of 24.3% ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , while dynamic anonymization leaves residual leakage rates of 0.17 on ChatDoctor and 0.33 on EnronQA ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . Similarly, the multilingual input judge in Li et al. (2026b) blocks English extraction prompts but still leaves 7.5% residual leakage on Arabic queries and 17.5% on Swahili. These divergent numbers show that there is no universal exchange rate between privacy and accuracy in RAG generation. An operating point that looks safe on aggregate copying scores can still fail on specific entity types, non-English queries, or multi-turn extraction prompts. Consequently, studies evaluating Families A and A-pii must report their residual leakage alongside exact workload conditions and utility costs, rather than treating a drop in average text overlap as proof that source content cannot be extracted. 4.2 Source Reconstruction Outside Generation (Family B) Even if a RAG system never leaks a single word through its generated answers, an attacker can still reconstruct indexed documents through underlying system channels. Family B captures these non-generation reconstruction endpoints, accounting for 7 records in our map (and every record that reports a content-reconstruction metric). Research here targets three distinct leakage channels, each requiring its own defense style. The most widely studied channel is embedding inversion, where an adversary with access to stored vectors runs a trained decoder such as Vec2Text or a fine-tuned T5 model to recover the original text. Defenses against inversion either add entropy-driven perturbations to the vectors ( Jin et al., 2025 ) or apply distance-preserving and homomorphic encryption so the index remains searchable without exposing raw embeddings ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2026 ) . A second channel is index-structure and deletion residue: PRAG demonstrates that a semi-honest server observing HNSW graph traversal paths can reconstruct the underlying document graph without inspecting a single vector ( Li et al., 2026c ) , while Ghost Vectors reveals that soft-deleted embeddings linger in HNSW indices and remain invertible until the index is rebuilt ( Chakraborttii et al., 2026 ) . The third channel is parametric residue, which arises when retrieved knowledge is compressed into distilled LoRA weights rather than passed as text context, turning the adapter weights themselves into an inversion target ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Reversing this threat model, one study treats the vector store as an exfiltration medium and uses outlier detectors to catch steganographically smuggled embeddings ( Wanger, 2026 ) . Interpreting reconstruction scores in Family B requires paying close attention to both the reference object and the strength of the attacker’s decoder. Across the seven studies, defenses measure success against very different targets: distance-preserving encryption drives Vec2Text reconstruction BLEU down from 83 to 12 ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , path-oblivious retrieval cuts HNSW edge recovery from 18.3% to 6.8% alongside a measurable drop in retrieval recall ( Li et al., 2026c ) , and epoch-key rotation reduces ROUGE-L recovery from soft-deleted vectors from 0.207 to 0.000 ( Chakraborttii et al., 2026 ) . Because recovering source wording, graph edges, and deleted vectors are distinct events, these numbers cannot be compared on a single scale. More importantly, a near-zero reconstruction score is only meaningful if the baseline attack actually works on the unprotected system. In the clinical-note experiment of Chakraborttii et al. (2026) , for example, the unprotected baseline yields a Vec2Text ROUGE-L of just 0.009 because the off-the-shelf inverter struggles with domain-specific medical text; in such cases, a low defended score reflects a weak attacker rather than a strong defense. Finally, Family B endpoints are strictly orthogonal to generation endpoints: encrypting embeddings or hiding HNSW traversal paths protects the backend datastore, but it does nothing to stop the language model from quoting retrieved passages verbatim to an end user (Family A). 4.3 Mathematical Bounds and Likelihood Proxies (Family C) Instead of measuring actual text leakage or document reconstruction, the 6 records in Family C evaluate privacy through theoretical guarantees or statistical proxies, and every record in this family pairs its privacy metric with a task utility score. These studies fall into two distinct groups. The formal sub-family injects calibrated noise into the RAG pipeline and tracks a mathematical privacy budget. Within this group, DP-RDM adapts retrieval-augmented diffusion models to private domains under a differential privacy budget of ε = 10 \varepsilon=10 ( Golatkar et al., 2024 ; Lebensold et al., 2024 ) , while Private-RAG uses individual Rényi privacy filters to answer hundreds of queries at ε ≈ 10 \varepsilon\approx 10 in settings where naive composition would require ε ≈ 1000 \varepsilon\approx 1000 ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . Other formal approaches apply differential privacy directly to token voting during text generation ( Koga et al., 2024 ) or use pure ε \varepsilon -DP SimHash bucketing when building the retrieval datastore ( Abouelenein and Torki, 2026 ) . By contrast, the statistical sub-family measures privacy through changes in model likelihood rather than formal bounds: SILO evaluates nonparametric datastores by comparing the model’s perplexity on a held-out book when related books are present in the index versus when they are removed, treating the likelihood shift itself as the primary endpoint ( Min et al., 2024 ) . While mathematical bounds and likelihood shifts offer clean theoretical targets, they do not measure what a deployed system actually emits to a user, and their numbers cannot be pooled with empirical leakage rates. Even within Family C, reported operating points depend heavily on the protected unit, the composition rule, and the query workload. For example, DP-RDM achieves its ε = 10 \varepsilon=10 guarantee over T = 100 T=100 k queries with a generation FID of 155.67 ( Lebensold et al., 2024 ) , whereas Private-RAG maintains ε ≈ 10 \varepsilon\approx 10 by permanently retiring individual documents from retrieval once their personal privacy budgets are exhausted ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . Meanwhile, the private datastore approach in Abouelenein and Torki (2026) translates its SimHash bucketing guarantee into an empirical audit, reducing membership-inference accuracy from 70.22% to 53.60% at the cost of a 2.6% drop in task accuracy. Because query budgets, neighboring-dataset definitions, and utility trade-offs vary so widely across these setups, a paper reporting ε = 10 \varepsilon=10 and a paper reporting zero verbatim copied spans (Family A) are providing fundamentally different types of evidence, even when evaluated on the exact same corpus. 4.4 Access and Retrieval Suppression (Family D) Rather than scoring the words in a generated answer, Family D evaluates whether restricted documents are retrieved, routed, or allowed to be answered in the first place. Containing 26 records, this is the largest content-adjacent family in our map, and 96% of its studies report net improvements. Defenses here differ primarily in where they enforce authorization along the pipeline, and their results point to a clear engineering rule: enforcing access checks late in the pipeline is far riskier than enforcing them early. The common retrieve-then-filter pattern, which fetches top- k k passages first and checks permissions afterward, still exposes unauthorized context in 86.1% of base queries ( Namboothiri, 2026 ) . By contrast, pushing authorization down into the database engine through row-level security or predicate pushdown eliminates cross-tenant retrieval leakage entirely ( Budigi and Sirigiri, 2026 ; Arceo and Narsing, 2026 ) . Beyond structural database rules, a second group of defenses relies on semantic or learned policies, filtering passages by inferred user role, governing access at retrieval time, or placing a policy firewall around the RAG pipeline ( Lorenzo et al., 2025 ; Nutakki, 2026 ; Yao et al., 2025a ) . A third group modifies the system architecture or the documents themselves, either isolating the communication channel so raw user prompts never meet protected sources inside the generator ( Cherubin and Paverd, 2025 ) or perturbing source texts so a retrieving model cannot extract usable answers from them ( Agnew et al., 2024 ) . Notably, RAG unlearning studies that measure success by how often the model refuses to answer forbidden questions also fall into Family D rather than a removal category ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . Comparing operating points across Family D highlights a sharp divide between deterministic permission checks and learned semantic filters. When access policies are tied to clean database metadata, engine-level row security drives tenant-isolation leakage from 0.2% down to zero across 1,000 queries ( Budigi and Sirigiri, 2026 ) . However, when permissions must be inferred from natural language or when metadata is imperfect, residual leakage quickly reappears. For example, the AI-driven role filter in ARBITER reaches 85% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.89 over 389 queries, which actually trails the 0.93 to 0.94 F1 achieved by a simple static filter ( Lorenzo et al., 2025 ) . Similarly, hybrid graph-retrieval defenses remain vulnerable when 5% to 10% of document metadata labels are randomly corrupted ( Thornton, 2026a ) , and enterprise confidentiality filters see their recall drop to 74.35% when user queries omit explicit project names ( Byun et al., 2025 ) . More fundamentally, suppressing access or answerability is not the same as preventing content disclosure. On the one hand, a refusal rate measures policy compliance rather than whether sensitive knowledge was truly erased from the system. On the other hand, achieving zero unauthorized retrieval says nothing about what happens when the user is authorized. In commercial or licensed RAG deployments, legitimate subscribers are permitted to retrieve from the datastore, yet the operator must still prevent the model from reproducing copyrighted chapters verbatim. Protecting against that risk requires evaluating emitted expression (Family A) alongside retrieval permissions. 4.5 Post-Hoc Corpus-Use Detection (Family E) Instead of blocking queries or suppressing generated text, the 18 records in Family E ask a forensic question: can an auditor prove after the fact that a specific document collection was indexed or queried by a RAG system? Strikingly, most studies framed around copyright and dataset ownership concentrate in this family, even though usage detection does not measure or prevent content disclosure. Research here follows four technical paths depending on whether the auditor can modify the corpus beforehand. The dominant design plants a verifiable signal into the data and later probes the suspect system to recover it. Researchers have embedded these signals as statistical watermarks in generated text ( Jovanović et al., 2025 ) , dual-layer semantic and lexical watermarks ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , reasoning traces in chain-of-thought space ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , multi-bit ownership payloads ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , black-box knowledge base watermarks ( Lv et al., 2025 ) , synthetic sentinel documents ( Kwok et al., 2026 ) , retrievability-optimized canaries ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , visual sentinel images ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , and multimodal watermarks for RAG-as-a-Service platforms ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . When planting signals in advance is impossible, a second, signal-free group audits corpus membership directly through black-box queries ( Zeng et al., 2025b ) . Flipping the roles, a third group builds defenses to protect the datastore against membership inference attacks ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) , while a fourth inspects internal model activations or runtime execution games to catch unauthorized extraction ( Zhang et al., 2025c ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . Evaluating Family E endpoints requires separating the reliability of the forensic signal from the secrecy of the underlying text. First, detection scores are highly sensitive to calibration choices, query budgets, the fraction of target material actually indexed, and simple post-processing attacks. For example, the watermark detector in Ward begins to trigger false positives when only 20% of the watermarked document set is present in the target corpus ( Jovanović et al., 2025 ) . Under adversarial paraphrasing, membership audit performance in Zeng et al. (2025b) drops to an AUC of 79.6%. Similarly, applying a detect-and-inpaint filter causes visual sentinel detection to fall from an AUC of 0.99 to 0.62 ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , while injecting external knowledge into the database cuts RAG-WM watermark integrity from 100% down to 46.67% ( Lv et al., 2025 ) . Comparing detectors therefore requires matching their false-positive thresholds and adversarial post-processing budgets. Second, and more fundamentally, a usage detector is an alarm rather than a lock: proving that a document sits inside a remote index says nothing about whether its protected wording was ever emitted to an end user (Family A), nor whether an attacker could reconstruct that wording without triggering the alarm. 4.6 Pipeline Integrity, Attribution, and Recurring Failure Modes (Family F) Accounting for 47 records (40% of our entire map), Family F is by far the largest endpoint category, covering defenses against corpus poisoning, prompt injection, and provenance failures. Rather than protecting the secrecy of indexed documents, these endpoints test whether the RAG pipeline returns trustworthy, uncorrupted answers and correctly credits its sources. Poisoning defenses intervene at three stages of the pipeline. Admission-time filters screen out malicious documents before they enter the index using perplexity scores, Mahalanobis distance, vector hubness, or inter-document similarity ( Cheng et al., 2025b ; Xian et al., 2024 ; Pathak and Sharma, 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . Retrieval-time defenses re-rank candidate passages, partition the retrieved set, or analyze context structure to isolate corrupted chunks ( Pathmanathan et al., 2025 ; Saxena et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2025b ) . Generation-time defenses aggregate answers across multiple passages, sometimes providing formal robustness certificates under a bounded poisoning budget, or isolate untrusted spans during synthesis ( Tan et al., 2026 ; Sharma, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Alongside poisoning defenses, prompt-injection studies enforce runtime control-flow integrity or deploy layered input scanners ( Saleem et al., 2026 ; Alam et al., 2026 ) , while a separate attribution literature traces poisoned outputs back to responsible documents, localizes corrupted spans at the character level, or uses internal model states to verify answer provenance ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Cui and Liu, 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Qi et al., 2024 ) . Comparing evaluation practices in Family F against the rest of the map reveals a telling contrast. Because poisoning and injection studies draw heavily from adversarial machine learning, 51% of Family F records receive a low-concern rating for adaptive robustness testing, and 45% explicitly document an adaptive attack among their failure modes. For example, while a non-adaptive guardrail reports a true-positive rate of 1.000 at a false-positive rate of 0.015 ( Cohen et al., 2024 ) , adaptive white-box attacks like PoisonedRAG-W push document-detector false-negative rates up to roughly 96% ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , and consistency collusion bypasses 70.3% of multi-agent audits ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Yet despite this strong tradition of adaptive testing, zero records in Family F document an attacker recovering protected source content against the proposed defense. The reason is simple: in Family F, an attack success rate (ASR) measures whether the attacker tricked the system into outputting a targeted wrong answer, executing a hijacked instruction, or citing the wrong source. Keeping ASR at zero guarantees that the pipeline behaves as the operator intended, but it is completely compatible with a system that answers every user query by quoting its private or copyrighted sources verbatim. Looking across all seven endpoint families (Families A, A-pii, and B–F), three recurring evaluation patterns explain why reported operating points rarely transfer from one setting to another (Appendix D ). First, defenses face steep protection-utility trade-offs whose magnitudes are seldom reported on a shared scale ( Zeng et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Second, claims of zero residual leakage almost always depend on fragile assumptions, such as perfectly clean permission metadata or attackers who explicitly name their target entities in the query ( Nutakki, 2026 ; Chakraborttii et al., 2026 ) . Third, moving from static queries to adaptive attackers routinely overturns the apparent success of a defense ( Yao et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) . These recurring limitations point to deeper structural gaps in how RAG protection is designed and evaluated, which we audit next. 5 Three Blind Spots in RAG Protection Research Stepping back from individual endpoint families, our evidence map allows us to audit how the RAG protection literature as a whole connects methods, claims, and evaluations. Reading the 118 human-coded studies across families exposes three systemic blind spots that explain why progress in this field is so difficult to compare. 5.1 Blind Spot I: Mechanisms Do Not Dictate Endpoints When readers encounter a RAG defense that “reranks retrieved passages” or “rewrites context before generation,” they naturally assume the mechanism tells them what risk is being mitigated.
